name: 5 Magazine
description: 5 Magazine is a Chicago house-music magazine published since August 2005 under editor Czarina Mirani, also known as Czboogie. It appears as a free monthly print edition distributed across Chicago, alongside a digital edition, billing itself "North America's only magazine dedicated exclusively to house music." It became the print and digital chronicler of Chicago house music's second and third generations, documenting the DJs, labels, and parties the mainstream press ignored. Resident Advisor marked the magazine's tenth anniversary in 2015 with a Victor Simonelli event.

name: 2Pac
aliases: Makaveli; Tupac Amaru Shakur; Tupac Shakur
description: Tupac Shakur, born in East Harlem, New York, in 1971 and raised in part in Baltimore and California, was a rapper, actor and writer whose work joined street reporting, political anger, tenderness and self-examination. The son of Afeni Shakur, he first recorded with Digital Underground before his solo debut, 2Pacalypse Now, in 1991. Albums including Strictly 4 My N.I.G.G.A.Z., Me Against the World and the double album All Eyez on Me made him one of the defining artists of 1990s hip-hop, while film roles in Juice and Poetic Justice widened his reach. Songs such as Dear Mama, later selected for the National Recording Registry, and California Love remain central to his catalogue. Shakur was shot in Las Vegas on September 7, 1996, and died six days later, aged twenty-five. His influence did not end with his death: posthumous releases continued for years, and he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2017. CultureTechLens records him with gratitude for a body of work that still teaches listeners how contradiction, vulnerability and protest can live in the same voice.

name: 12-inch dance single
description: The 12-inch single — with its extended mixes and DJ-friendly format — was the commercial vehicle of Chicago house, from Trax and DJ International pressings to white-label circulation. The format itself was born of a 1974 studio accident: Tom Moulton and mastering engineer José Rodriguez cut a disco single on a 12-inch blank, spreading the grooves for louder, deeper club sound.

Supersedes the earlier "18% of 2020–2022" figure, which the Pew report does not support (see conflict CTL-CFL-001855).

name: 47th Street shopping and strolling — Bronzeville's Black consumer corridor
description: Everyday shopping, errand-running, and social promenading along 47th Street — especially 47th & South Parkway (now King Drive) — the commercial and social heart of Bronzeville. By the end of the Depression, 47th Street had replaced 35th & State as the Black Metropolis downtown; residents could shop, bank, and insure without leaving the Black Belt. Anchored by the Regal Theater (opened 1928, torn down 1973).

name: "Don't Spend Your Money Where You Can't Work" boycott pickets on 47th Street
description: Teenagers and adults picketing stores on 47th Street that served Black shoppers but refused to hire Black workers, 1929–1939. Created by James Hale Porter, Chicago Whip founder Joseph D. Bibb (who coined the slogan), and the NAACP's A.C. MacNeal, the campaign used daily picketing and boycotts — the first direct action among Black Chicago civil-rights organizations — and promoted the Double Duty Dollar.

name: "Don't Spend Your Money Where You Can't Work" campaign
description: Chicago-originated (1929) consumer boycott campaign, organized by the Chicago Whip (founder Joseph D. Bibb, managing editor A.C. MacNeal) and activist James Hale Porter with the NAACP. Slogan coined by Bibb; targeted A&P and Silver Dollar Food grocery chains with picketing and daily boycotts to force hiring of Black workers. First use of direct action among Black Chicago civil rights organizations.

name: "Six-hour dollar" circulation claim (DEBUNKED)
description: The widely repeated statistic that a dollar circulates six hours in the Black community. Earliest traced source: Brooke Stephens's 1996 book 'Talking Dollars and Making Sense,' which names no study. Howard University's TruthBeTold.news investigated and could not substantiate it; economists William Spriggs and Justin Wolfers call it an urban myth — the federal government produces no data allowing such comparisons. Still repeated as fact in Black economic discourse.

name: 79th Street commercial corridor (Chatham / Greater Grand Crossing)

Johnson in 1964, anchored the corridor at 79th and Cottage Grove, and the corridor included Black-owned financial institutions, theatres (Avalon/New Regal) and retail.

name: 87th Street commercial development (Chatham / Auburn Gresham)

name: 12 Years a Slave
description: 12 Years a Slave, directed by Steve McQueen from John Ridley's screenplay adapting Solomon Northup's 1853 memoir, and distributed in the United States by Fox Searchlight Pictures, tells the true account of a free Black man of New York kidnapped in 1841 and sold into Louisiana slavery for twelve years. At the 86th Academy Awards it won Best Picture, Best Adapted Screenplay for Ridley, and Best Supporting Actress for Lupita Nyong'o; it also won the Golden Globe for Best Motion Picture — Drama and the BAFTA for Best Film. Trade reporting put its worldwide gross at about $140 million on a reported $20 million budget. The Library of Congress selected it for the National Film Registry in 2023, a decade after release — the institution's confirmation of what the awards season had asserted. For this graph, whose timeline begins with the arrival of the enslaved in 1619, McQueen's film is the slavery era's defining screen treatment: unflinching where the textbook tradition was evasive, and sourced — a memoir, a named man, a recoverable record — in a way the citation standard can stand behind.
